title: Presidential War Powers: Executive Expansion and Congressional Retreat

ARTICLES

## Presidential War Powers: Executive Expansion and Congressional Retreat

Jeh Charles Johnson* and Ethan P. Klaris**

ABSTRACT

This paper provides a comprehensive and definitive account of the history of American war powers from the Founding to the present day. Drawing on constitu tional text, historical practice, statutory frameworks, judicial doctrine, and original interviews with present and former members of Congress, it reconstructs how the Constitution’s intended allocation of authority over war has steadily unraveled. The erosion of congressional war powers, the paper argues, is the product of both presidential ambition and congressional acquiescence across multiple generations. The paper proceeds in three parts. It begins by recalling the Framers’ origi nal design, which placed Congress at the center of decisions to initiate hostil ities. It then traces, in historical and empirical detail, the progressive expansion of presidential warmaking authority from the early Republic through Korea, Vietnam, the War Powers Resolution, the post-9/11 Authorizations for Use of Military Force, and the modern era of perpetual, unauthorized conflict. Finally, it offers contemporary proposals for reform and explains why restoring the con stitutional balance has proven so difficult in practice. By offering a unified historical account grounded in law, politics, and lived institutional experience, this paper supplies a comprehensive foundation for understanding—and evaluating—the modern law of war powers.

INTRODUCTION

The Constitution’s intended balance between the legislative and executive branches 
on matters of war powers is broken. Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution, which 
assigns to Congress the power to declare war, is a near nullity.

Neither political branch of government is solely to blame 
for this; they both are. Over the years, Congress has effectively abandoned its 
constitutional responsibility, and the President—in the name of national security, 
real or perceived—has filled it. 
This trend has accelerated in recent decades. Though the United States contin 
ues to deploy lethal military force to counter various security threats around the 
world, it has been twenty-four years since Congress has actually voted to author 
ize war. 
3 
The 2002 vote to go to war against Iraq—which came to be viewed as a 
grave mistake based on flawed intelligence—taught members of Congress that 
voting for war in all but the most compelling of circumstances can be hazardous 
to one’s political health.

In the absence of congressional action, successive presidents of both parties have 
filled the war powers vacuum. Executive branch attorneys have supplied the neces 
sary legal justifications for ever-expanding interpretations of executive authority to 
commit the armed forces into hostilities without congressional authorization. 
5

traditional view, embraced by the Supreme Court in The Prize Cases 6 and reflected

in the 1973 War Powers Resolution,

authority to defend the Nation from an armed invasion without prior congressional 
authorization.

Over the years, however, the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel (“OLC”) has gone far beyond this view, issuing opinions declaring that the President has constitutional authority to commit the armed forces to serve “impor tant national interests,” so long as the engagement does not rise to the level of a war in nature, scope and duration. 9 “ ” “ ”

What’s in the “national interest” is a policy judgment, not a legal one to be second-guessed by lawyers. Given the scarcity of judicial precedent in the war powers space, OLC engages in the practice of citing past unilateral uses of force as legal precedent for future ones—a doctrine known as “historical gloss.” But this method, too, offers no limiting principle and serves as a one-way ratchet upward. As commentators note, each unilateral inter vention enters the “grab-bag of past legal violations . . . stitched together to create a new rule at variance with the text of the Constitution.” 11

The cumulative effect of this 
expanding archive of executive authority is to constantly broaden the constitutional 
boundary line. To the layman, “historical gloss” must sound like declaring that, when 
motorists repeatedly drive eighty-five miles per hour in a sixty-five miles per hour 
zone, eighty-five miles per hour becomes the new legal speed limit. 
Generations of unilateralist presidential action have culminated in President 
Donald Trump’s second term, with the bombing of Iran’s nuclear enrichment 
facilities in June 2025, airstrikes to summarily kill suspected drug couriers on 
the high seas beginning in September 2025,

As of this writing, a fragile ceasefire agreement exists. The ripple effects of the war in Iran have included renewed violence across the Middle East, a chokehold on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, and a sudden, dramatic increase in gas prices in the United States. Though there is no doubt U.S. military operations in Iran constitute a “war,” Congress cannot do any thing to stop it. Repeated efforts to invoke the War Powers Resolution have failed largely along party lines. As President Trump likes to put it, he “holds all the cards.” 15

This article traces, from the beginning, the steady erosion of the constitutional balance between Congress and the President regarding war powers. But the overall trend away from congressional 
authorization and toward unilateral executive action is unmistakable. 
This trend in war powers is part of a broader interbranch history in which presi 
dents, frustrated by congressional inaction on their agenda, have increasingly asserted 
unilateral authority on matters where both Congress and the President should share 
responsibility. President Obama’s 2014 executive actions on immigration reform and 
President Biden’s 2022 executive actions to forgive federal student loan debt, both of 
which were declared invalid by the U.S. Supreme Court, are recent examples of 
this. 
18 
In his second term, President Trump has taken unilateral executive action to a 
new and even more audacious level. 
This is a law review article, but it is a story of both law and politics. For this 
work the authors had the benefit of exclusive interviews with present and former 
members of Congress: current Senator Tim Kaine, current Congressman (and for 
mer House Judiciary Committee Chair) Jerry Nadler, current Congressman (and 
former House Armed Services Committee Chair) Adam Smith, former House 
Majority Leader Dick Gephardt, former Senator (and former Secretary of Defense) 
Chuck Hagel, former Congressman (and former Secretary of Defense) Leon Panetta, 
and former Congresswoman Liz Holtzman. 
Collectively, these interviews conveyed a sober, real-life assessment of any 
effort to try to put the war powers toothpaste back in the constitutional tube. As 
Congressman Adam Smith told us, “[t]here is no practical way for Congress to
